stages.title: Start with the problem
stages.outcome: Tell a lookup, a learned prediction, and generated content apart.
stages.evidence: A four-line problem brief with a simple baseline.

questions.prompt: You need to find a book by its exact ID. What should you try first?
choices: Train a language model
Look up the ID in a table
Create three agents
questions.explanation: An exact lookup directly solves this problem. A model adds uncertainty without an established benefit.

questions.prompt: What does a fluent generated sentence establish?
choices: It is factually correct
It came from a current source
It is readable; its claims still need checking
questions.explanation: Fluency and truth are different properties. Check the claim against suitable evidence.

lessons.title: What AI is, and what you will build

stages.title: Write your first programs
stages.outcome: Use Python, tests, files, SQL, arrays, and charts to explain a dataset.
stages.evidence: A reading-log audit with validation, a chart, and repeatable checks.

questions.prompt: One row has no measured loan count. How should it be represented?
choices: As missing, with an explicit handling rule
As zero in every report
Remove the branch without mentioning it
questions.explanation: Missing means unknown; zero means a measured absence. Report the rule and affected count.

questions.prompt: A branch lookup table has duplicate keys. What can a join do?
choices: Always choose the correct row
Multiply matching rows and distort totals
Automatically repair the source
questions.explanation: Test key uniqueness and the intended join relationship before trusting aggregate totals.

lessons.title: Numbers, units, and the symbols you will meet
Computers, files, and your first program
Python values, names, and clear calculations
Decisions, loops, and reusable functions
Collections, records, and files
Debugging, input checks, and useful tests
Save your work and reproduce your environment
Data tables, SQL, and a complete data-audit project
From Python lists to arrays, tables, and charts

stages.title: Reason with numbers and uncertainty
stages.outcome: Trace shapes, gradients, probabilities, experiments, and compression.
stages.evidence: A comparison report with units, assumptions, and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a detector can ignore the base rate?
choices: The fraction of flags that are genuine
The probability of the event given a flag
Neither of those statements
questions.explanation: The population frequency affects both quantities. Use Bayes' rule with the relevant base rate.

questions.prompt: PCA retains a high-variance direction. What is guaranteed?
choices: It preserves all task-relevant information
It retains variation under its objective, not necessarily the best predictive feature
It proves two visible clusters are different classes
questions.explanation: Variance and task relevance are distinct. Measure downstream quality and rare cases.

lessons.title: Vectors and matrices: give numbers a structure
Functions, slopes, and gradient-based improvement
Probability, data summaries, and conditional questions
Experiments, uncertainty, and an evidence-audit project
Update beliefs and measure information
Linear transformations and useful compression

stages.title: Train and evaluate predictors
stages.outcome: Frame a task, train baselines, avoid leakage, and evaluate useful decisions.
stages.evidence: A reproducible prediction experiment with slice errors and a time-aware split.

questions.prompt: Where should a preprocessing scale be fitted?
choices: All rows before splitting
The final test set
Training data, then applied unchanged to evaluation data
questions.explanation: Fitting transformations on held-out data can leak information even without labels.

questions.prompt: A model reports 0.9 probability on many cases but the event occurs in half. What should you inspect?
choices: Probability calibration and the sample size
Only classification accuracy
The number of layers first
questions.explanation: Calibration compares probabilities with observed frequencies. A tiny sample gives weak evidence.

lessons.title: Frame a problem before choosing a model
Build features without leaking the answer
Fit a regression model with gradients
Classify outcomes and choose useful metrics
Learn decisions with trees and ensembles
Find groups and recommend useful items
Validate a model and finish the ML project
Trust scores, thresholds, and forecasts

stages.title: Understand neural networks
stages.outcome: Calculate gradients and explain training, vision, attention, and reward.
stages.evidence: A trained tiny network, gradient check, and error analysis.

questions.prompt: When should the two weights in a backward pass be updated?
choices: Update the first before calculating the second gradient
After calculating both gradients from the same forward pass
Whenever a partial result is ready
questions.explanation: Both derivatives must describe the original parameter state. Early updates mix different calculations.

questions.prompt: Why mask future tokens during causal language-model training?
choices: To prevent using information unavailable during generation
To remove every form of uncertainty
To avoid learning from earlier tokens
questions.explanation: At generation time the future tokens do not yet exist. The training information boundary must match.

lessons.title: Build a neural network from small operations
Backpropagation, one multiplication at a time
Train carefully with and without PyTorch
Learn visual patterns with convolutions
Understand sequences and calculate attention
Put attention inside a Transformer
Learn actions from rewards and finish the stage

stages.title: Generate and validate content
stages.outcome: Explain tokens, prompts, adaptation, multimodal inputs, and decoding.
stages.evidence: A controlled generation experiment and a preference-labeling rubric.

questions.prompt: An output passes JSON parsing. What has been established?
choices: The facts and permissions are correct
The syntax is valid; meaning still needs checks
The model is calibrated
questions.explanation: Structural validation is one layer. Verify fields, source support, and authorized actions separately.

questions.prompt: What changes when you lower a positive sampling temperature?
choices: The model learns new facts
Its parameters are fine-tuned
The next-token distribution becomes sharper
questions.explanation: Temperature changes selection from the current logits, not learned model weights or factual guarantees.

lessons.title: Language models: predicting the next piece
Prompts and structured output
Adaptation: prompts, retrieval, and fine-tuning
Multimodal generation and a tiny language-model project
Choose tokens and teach preferred behavior

stages.title: Train and adapt language models
stages.outcome: Prepare data, train a small model, reload it, and justify adaptation.
stages.evidence: A checkpoint, split manifest, held-out results, and model card.

questions.prompt: When should source documents be split?
choices: Before generating overlapping chunks or examples
After randomly mixing every chunk
After seeing final test results
questions.explanation: Source-level splitting helps prevent near-duplicates from leaking across partitions.

questions.prompt: Lower perplexity comes with more corrupted identifiers. What decides release?
choices: Perplexity alone
Task-specific gates including exact identifier preservation
The smaller checkpoint
questions.explanation: A general prediction metric can improve while a critical task requirement gets worse.

lessons.title: Choose what to build, train, and run
Prepare data, tokenizers, and prediction targets
Train, save, and reload a small neural language model
Fine-tune a model and evaluate the release

stages.title: Find evidence and ground answers
stages.outcome: Build, compare, and update permission-aware retrieval pipelines.
stages.evidence: A labeled query benchmark, supported answers, and freshness/access tests.

questions.prompt: Why fuse ranks rather than simply add unrelated retriever scores?
choices: Ranks eliminate all irrelevant results
Keyword and vector scores may use incompatible scales
Ranks are probabilities
questions.explanation: Rank fusion combines positions without assuming a shared numerical score scale.

questions.prompt: A citation points to a real document. What remains to check?
choices: Only the URL length
Nothing; the citation proves the answer
Whether the document supports the claim and is current and authorized
questions.explanation: Existence, support, freshness, and access are different requirements.

lessons.title: Retrieval basics: find evidence before answering
Indexing, chunks, and search choices
Grounded answers and honest uncertainty
RAG evaluation and an offline evidence-search project
Build and evaluate a hybrid retrieval pipeline

stages.title: Build bounded, recoverable agents
stages.outcome: Connect models to validated tools and resume actions safely.
stages.evidence: A model-agent fixture suite, bounded execution, and a crash/retry trace.

questions.prompt: A write times out after it may have succeeded. What is the first response?
choices: Repeat with a new action key
Ask the model whether it probably worked
Mark the result uncertain and reconcile the original action
questions.explanation: A lost response does not establish failure. Check the authoritative receipt before retrying.

questions.prompt: A tool result says to bypass approval. What authority does it have?
choices: It is data and cannot change the application's policy
It overrides the user because it came from a tool
It can grant permission if repeated twice
questions.explanation: Tool output is not a trusted instruction channel. Authorization belongs to application code.

lessons.title: Tools, workflows, and agents
The agent loop: state, actions, and stopping
Multiple agents: divide work only when it helps
Agent evaluation and a bounded offline project
Build an agent that uses a real model
Connect agents to real applications
Resume an agent without repeating its actions

stages.title: Build conversational applications
stages.outcome: Maintain sessions, connect channels, and test multi-turn behavior.
stages.evidence: A browser bot with session isolation, fallback, and channel tests.

questions.prompt: A messaging channel redelivers the same event. What should identify the duplicate?
choices: The text alone
A stable event ID under a documented deduplication policy
A newly generated random ID each time
questions.explanation: Stable identities let retries represent the same logical event. Text can repeat legitimately.

questions.prompt: A bot test passes with scripted replies. What does that establish?
choices: All live model answers are accurate
The live model never uses forbidden tools
The tested application behavior under those fixtures
questions.explanation: Fixture tests are deterministic boundary evidence; live quality needs a separate evaluation.

lessons.title: Choose and design the right kind of bot
Build a working local chatbot, then connect a model
Connect a bot to messaging channels
Test whole conversations and operate a bot responsibly

stages.title: Operate reliable AI systems
stages.outcome: Release, secure, monitor, budget, and benchmark an AI service.
stages.evidence: A release gate, workload report, token budget, and rollback demonstration.

questions.prompt: A system rejects many requests and reports low latency. What is missing?
choices: Acceptance, rejection, error rates, and the workload definition
Only a larger model
A different color for the dashboard
questions.explanation: Latency alone can hide dropped work. Define success over the relevant traffic boundary.

questions.prompt: A smaller quantized cache makes short requests slower. Is that possible?
choices: No; fewer bits always means faster
Yes; conversion overhead can exceed memory savings
Only if the input contains no tokens
questions.explanation: Measure latency, memory, and quality independently on the intended workload.

lessons.title: Serve a model through an API
Evaluate releases and monitor real use
Protect data and define responsibility
Design an AI system and release it deliberately
Manage token and context budgets
Develop reliable AI applications and code with AI
Make inference fast without hiding its costs

stages.title: Make defensible research claims
stages.outcome: Reproduce a result, isolate a change, and report uncertainty and limits.
stages.evidence: A research report with matched baselines, ablations, and an experiment ledger.

questions.prompt: Students who chose an assistant read more. What does that prove?
choices: The assistant caused the increase
No association exists
An association; motivation may confound the causal claim
questions.explanation: People self-select. A causal interpretation needs a suitable design and stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: You choose the best of 40 prompts on the final test set. What is that set now?
choices: Development data used for selection
Still an untouched final test
A randomized trial
questions.explanation: Selection used its information. Freeze the procedure and evaluate on fresh untouched examples.

lessons.title: Read a paper and test its claim
Understand training and inference at scale
Choose a research question and run an independent experiment
From a promising result to a defensible research claim

stages.title: Prepare your independent capstone
stages.outcome: Choose a role, define acceptance gates, and defend alternatives.
stages.evidence: One reviewed professional studio and a reproducible handoff.

questions.prompt: Which portfolio claim is strongest?
choices: A list of frameworks used
A working project with a baseline, failure evidence, and reproducible evaluation
A claim that all questions are solved
questions.explanation: Evidence allows reviewers to assess behavior and limits independently of tool names.

questions.prompt: A critical permission test fails but the overall rubric score is high. What follows?
choices: Average away the failure
Skip the test next time
Fix the critical boundary before claiming readiness
questions.explanation: Critical requirements are gates, not interchangeable points in an average.
